Math is literally the most verifiable domain there is, more verifiable than even coding. That's why these things have been set to work in math first and so effectively.

The point of mathematics is not to teach more human mathematicians and create textbooks and produce seminars. It is to advance the surface area of knowledge. 

If LLMs are doing that without us, all the better.

If the objection was "don't steal results and attribute them properly" then I'd be the first to rush to agreement. I've been calling out & documenting the Navier-Stokes drama, so I'm with you there.

But that's mostly an OpenAI problem, not an AI solving math problems problem. Stealing results is a minor quibble in this letter, and is not the thrust of the objection.

From the letter:

The mathematical community functions, in many ways, as a miniature version of humanity. It consists of individuals using a wide variety of different approaches, joined by core values. The most precious resources of our profession are students and ideas, and these we nurture with great care. We feel responsible to let them grow to their full potential, until they can live a life of their own in the mathematical world. For students we often suggest problems with the core intention of developing skills making them well-positioned for advances in research and elsewhere. Our ideas we disseminate in talks, private discussions and careful writeups, connecting them to the previous ideas of others. These processes invariably take time and are based on human interaction.

In recent months, the success of AI in solving major mathematical problems has made headlines even outside mathematical circles. But solving problems is only a tool and proxy for achieving the primary goal of conceptual understanding and insight. Forgetting this in the world of AI may turn the tool against the primary goal. Indeed, the mass production at faster and faster pace of "true/false" statements could destroy fertile ground instead of breathing life into new ideas.

The classic way to blow up a startup was throwing too much money at it. Hire a thousand people, create dueling priorities, and kill what was working.

thread_tweets.text:
It's been a long journey getting here:

Numbers reported directly by projects tend to be wrong cause projects are incentivized to show high APYs to attract capital

So then you decide let's get data from onchain only by reading pricePerShare or equivalent. But there are pools with slippage on withdrawal for larger amounts, pools with low withdrawal liquidity, and pools where the number is just wrong cause of fees

Then we started depositing into pools directly to benchmark real yield, but we missed historical data, the APY could be faked if our address was targeted, and your deposits are so low that you might be able to exit any time but someone with 10m cant, so you can't tell if its liquid

By simulating withdrawal transactions from all depositors we completely eliminate any possibility of cheating, we know exactly how much everyone is earning, how much could be instantly withdrawn if there's a bank run, we even simulate multiple stage withdrawals so we know exactly how long the delays are in those cases.

I think this is the end game, we now have perfectly accurate data so you can trust our numbers (rn its only rolled out for pools with the verified badge, but rolling out to everything soon)

⚡ THE DAILY METALS PULSE | 11 SEPTEMBER 2026 ⚡
Four metals. One pulse. No noise.

CPI delivered the expected inflation shock.

US consumer prices rose 0.4% in August, with core inflation increasing 0.3%. Markets now price an 87% probability of a Fed hike next week.

But something interesting happened after the initial selloff:

Gold and silver reversed higher.

☢️ URANIUM

Numerco’s latest public physical OTC U₃O₈ indication remains around $90/lb.

A separate benchmark-linked financial reference increased to $90.20. That is not a completed physical spot transaction, and neither price should be confused with uranium miners or listed trusts.

As the World Nuclear Symposium concludes, the conversation is shifting from whether nuclear will expand to how that expansion will be financed.

The uranium move remains intact. Fresh physical transactions must now confirm it.

🟠 COPPER

Copper is around $6.47/lb, while three-month LME copper has retreated toward $14,250 per tonne after reaching a record $14,875.

The trigger was political, not geological.

Washington’s hesitation over refined-copper tariffs rapidly removed the premium created by metal being redirected into US warehouses.

Copper may end its ten-week winning streak, but no new mines appeared during the selloff. The structural supply problem remains.

🥈 SILVER

Silver has rebounded approximately 1.6% to $64.50/oz, although it remains down around 2.6% this week.

Higher rates and copper’s reversal destroyed the breakout. Dip-buying after CPI prevented the decline from accelerating.

Silver has not regained momentum, but it has shown that investors are willing to defend it near $63–64.

🥇 GOLD

Gold has recovered approximately 1.1% to $4,363/oz despite the probability of a September rate hike rising to 87%.

That is the day’s most important signal.

Gold initially fell on inflation and higher yields. Buyers then stepped in while the US 10-year yield remained near 4.93%.

The market is still treating inflation as a reason for tighter policy. But gold’s reversal suggests investors are also beginning to remember why hard assets exist.

Hot CPI.
Near-certain rate hike.
Gold and silver still reversed higher.

The hard-asset trade took a hit this week.
It did not disappear.

Polymarket launched perps, and AI agents got more tools to trade with.

12 updates worth catching up on:

• @pendle_fi shipped an SDK for Boros, plus an API, contract Router access, a CLI, and delegated agent wallets. Boros is becoming an algo-tradeable venue.

• @PayBox added @JupiterExchange as a trading plugin, bringing Solana routing and pricing inside Claude, ChatGPT, and Grok conversations.

• @Mantle_Official became a @global_dollar Network partner, adding Paxos-issued USDG to its stablecoin stack.

• @LaunchOnSF moved new deployments onto @Raydium LaunchLab. Cuts deployment costs, reduces sniper risk, and keeps liquidity compounding after bonding.

• @superformxyz has integrated Robinhood Chain, opening its app to 170+ tokenized stocks and the chain's memecoin markets.

• @zestprotocol launched Levered Bitcoin Staking on @Stacks. The vault loops stBTC into more staking exposure without manual borrowing or rebalancing.

• @VenusProtocol launched Liquidity Hub on @BNBCHAIN. Deposit one asset, receive one hub token, and let governance-set strategies allocate across supported Venus markets.

• @strata_markets launched senior and junior tranches for Black Opal's LiquidStone II fund, which finances short-dated, FX-hedged Brazilian credit-card receivables.

• @kamino opened a ZEC-backed USDC market on Solana, curated by @AllezLabs. It's isolated, so ZEC collateral risk stays contained to its own market.

• @USDai_Official funded a $54.4M @get_hydrahost facility for 1,040 @nvidia B300 GPUs. Funds are released from escrow only after deployment verification.

Give an agent a Pendle wallet and Jupiter routing and it'll execute faster than you ever could. What it can't do yet is decide whether the trade was worth taking.

The tools are getting better every week. Judgement is the only thing left that doesn't ship in an SDK...well at least not yet.

@Jason:

“Should they trust any of these LLMs with their proprietary knowledge for fear of having it cribbed into a core LLM?”

@friedberg:

“I have had experiences where we've asked some fairly novel scientific questions, and (the AI model) identifies it as a novel insight.

It's like, ‘Oh, never thought about that, interesting, blah, blah, blah.’

And then using a different account, asking the next version (of the model) later, I've now experienced this.

It's like, ‘Oh, well, you could do this,’ and it actually just describes this exact thing that we had in our chat in the previous version.

Now, these are a handful of anecdotal experiences, but I know the domain that we work in, and the niche of it, and the ideation of this stuff, and the novelty of this stuff, and the lack of papers being published, and so on.

So I know that there isn't some new corpus of information out there that's training the new model.

So all I can say at that point is that my conversation or our analyses have been used for training.”

@DavidSacks:

“Okay, this does raise a really good question. What does it mean that the model is allowed to train on unidentifiable data?”

“Well, that's my point. So it doesn't use any of my personal information, but it can use an insight derived from our chat, which it can then say is some training data that is unrelated.

But the truth is, it's actually a piece of IP that's our organization’s IP, and our engagement back and forth. We don't have any NDA or confidentiality provisions or protections with them being a service provider back to us.

This is why I care a lot about open source because I don't want them having my chat logs because they can use it for training to create an IP advantage that is now diffused to the rest of the market.”

Before, they lived in my head all day: “I need to remember to message this person.” Now I just leave a voice note and the agent handles it.

The internet created a similar shift. We stopped memorizing everything and learned how to find information when we needed it, freeing our brains for more interesting work.

Agents are doing the same for life admin. It’s already such a huge improvement to my life, and we’re only getting started.
